title: Protect productive environments

blocks.heading: Protect productive environments
blocks.text: Conservation protects the resources and environmental conditions supporting rural lives and production. Immediate output gains from damaging soil, water or habitats can undermine future opportunities. Sustainable agriculture applies this wider development principle specifically to farming.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Land clearance
blocks.text: Clearing vegetation can create growing space but can expose soil and remove habitats. Where rain or wind acts on unprotected soil, loss of cover can increase erosion. Suitability depends on slope, remaining protection and the productive purpose.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Fuelwood
blocks.text: Wood is renewable where regrowth replaces harvesting under suitable conditions. Cutting faster than regeneration can deplete woodland, reduce future fuel access and expose soil. Efficient stoves and managed harvesting must fit users’ needs and maintenance capacity.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Erosion and degradation
blocks.text: Erosion removes soil; land degradation reduces productive condition through processes such as erosion, loss of fertility or damaging use. Reduced topsoil or vegetation can lower yields and increase vulnerability, so the response should match the cause rather than merely add more seed.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Agricultural pollution
blocks.text: Agricultural chemicals or wastes can reach soil and water through inappropriate use, storage or runoff. Where runoff carries pollutants into a shared source, downstream users and ecosystems may be affected. Safe management and suitable buffers address the pathway; more extraction does not.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Wildlife diversity
blocks.text: Wildlife diversity includes different species and habitats that support ecological relationships and other values. Habitat loss can reduce that diversity. Conservation should also consider local access, safety and livelihood costs rather than assuming benefits are shared equally.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Sustainable rural development
blocks.text: Sustainable rural development meets present needs while protecting future capacity to meet needs. An improvement can raise useful output by reducing waste rather than extracting more resources. Continued maintenance, inclusion and resource condition determine whether it lasts.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Protect useful output
blocks.text: Explain the rural-development mechanism in this fictional case: a storage repair reduces losses from 30 to 10 bags out of the same 100 harvested, with buyers available. Twenty more bags remain useful from unchanged harvesting. Reduced waste can support sales without more extraction, if storage maintenance continues.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Connect this lesson to Production (3.1), Sustainable Development (1.2) and Urbanisation (4.2). Identify the livelihood or resource constraint, trace the mechanism and distinguish a feasible action from a hoped-for outcome. The cases here are fictional, not claims about a named present-day community.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated
